questions.stem: What shape are the drawn field lines around a straight current-carrying wire?

options.explanation: The straight-wire pattern is concentric circles.

options.text: lines from end to end of the wire
options.explanation: End-to-end lines belong to bar magnets.
Parallel lines are the uniform-gap pattern.
The circles close on themselves; they do not spiral in.

questions.stem: A cross is drawn on the wire symbol in a field diagram. It means the current flows:

options.explanation: The cross marks a current, not its absence.
The cross is the tail feathers of an arrow going away.
Out is drawn as a dot, the arrow tip.

options.text: along the page to the right
options.explanation: In-page directions are drawn as arrows, not crosses.

questions.stem: How does the drawing show that the field weakens with distance from the wire?

options.explanation: Shape never changes — only spacing.
Spacing is exactly the strength encoding.

options.text: the circles are spaced further apart with distance
options.explanation: Wider spacing encodes weaker field.

options.text: the circles get smaller with distance
options.explanation: Circles get LARGER with radius; spacing is the cue.

questions.stem: A student draws the straight-wire pattern with the circles running the wrong way. Which check catches the error?

options.text: measuring the wire with a ruler
options.explanation: Wire length is unrelated to the circulation sense.
Circle count is a drawing choice, not a physics check.
Mass has no bearing on the field pattern.

options.text: applying the right-hand grip rule with the thumb along the current
options.explanation: The grip rule fixes the circulation sense.

questions.stem: Which diagram element is ESSENTIAL when drawing the straight-wire pattern?

options.text: the current direction marked with a cross or dot
options.explanation: Without the current label the circulation sense is undefined.
Circle count is a choice, not a requirement.
Colour carries no field meaning here.
The pattern of one wire stands alone.

questions.stem: State the shape and direction rule for the field pattern of a straight wire.
questions.modelAnswer: Circles centred on the wire, with the circulation direction given by the right-hand grip rule.

questions.stem: State the drawing convention for current into and out of the page.
questions.modelAnswer: A cross marks current into the page and a dot marks current out of the page.

questions.stem: Explain why the drawn circles are closest together right next to the wire.
questions.modelAnswer: Line spacing encodes field strength, and the field around a straight wire is strongest at the wire surface and weakens with distance. Drawing the circles crowded at the wire and increasingly spaced outward makes the strength falloff visible in the pattern itself.

questions.stem: Sketch-check: a wire carries current out of the page. State the circulation sense of the field circles as seen looking at the page, and name the rule used.
questions.modelAnswer: With the dot showing current towards the viewer, the grip rule gives anticlockwise circles as seen on the page — thumb pointing out at you, fingers curling anticlockwise. The rule used is the right-hand grip rule.

questions.stem: Why is the field at the centre of a flat coil stronger than one wire's field?

options.text: the centre is closer to the battery
options.explanation: Distance to the battery is irrelevant to the pattern.

options.text: every turn contributes field in the same direction there
options.explanation: The contributions add at the centre.

options.text: the coil stores charge at the centre
options.explanation: No charge accumulates; fields add, not charge.

options.text: the coil's wire is thicker at the centre
options.explanation: Wire thickness is uniform around the coil.

questions.stem: How are the field lines drawn through the CENTRE of a flat circular coil?

options.explanation: Field lines never cross.

options.text: absent — the centre has no field
options.explanation: The centre has the STRONGEST field.

options.text: nearly straight along the axis, crowded together
options.explanation: The centre field is strong and axial.
The central field has one clear direction.

questions.stem: Doubling the number of turns on a flat coil, keeping the current the same, does what to the central field?

options.explanation: More turns add, not subtract.
Direction follows the current sense, unchanged here.
Turn count is a strength factor.
More turns, more contributing fields.

questions.stem: The current in a flat coil is reversed. What happens to the drawn pattern?

options.text: the pattern is mirrored — every field direction reverses
options.explanation: The axial field flips to the other direction.
Arrows all reverse with the current.

options.text: the pattern becomes a straight-wire pattern
options.explanation: Shape follows geometry, not current sense.
The contributions still add — in the new direction.

questions.stem: Which statement about a single turn and a many-turn coil of the same radius and current is correct?

options.explanation: Both do — one weakly, one strongly.

options.text: the many-turn coil has the stronger central field
options.explanation: Turns stack the same-direction contributions.

options.text: the single turn has the stronger central field
options.explanation: Fewer contributions means a weaker total.
Turn count changes the sum.

questions.stem: State why the field lines through the coil centre point in one common direction.
questions.modelAnswer: Each turn of the coil gives a field contribution in the same axial direction at the centre, so they add to one common direction.

questions.stem: State two ways to strengthen the central field of a flat coil.
questions.modelAnswer: Add more turns to the coil or increase the current through it.

questions.stem: Explain why the drawn pattern of a flat coil looks like a bar magnet's field rather than a straight wire's.
questions.modelAnswer: The stacked turns give the coil two effective faces — field leaving one side and entering the other — like the poles of a bar magnet, so the external lines curl from face to face. A straight wire has no such faces: its field is pure circles with no pole structure to draw.

questions.stem: A flat coil of 40 turns carries 2 A; a second coil of 80 turns carries 1 A at the same radius. Compare the two central fields and justify the comparison.
questions.modelAnswer: The central field scales with turns times current, so the first coil gives 40 × 2 = 80 units and the second 80 × 1 = 80 units — the two central fields are equal in strength and point along the same axial geometry determined by each coil's winding sense.

questions.stem: The field pattern OUTSIDE a current-carrying solenoid resembles:

options.explanation: The solenoid has a full external field.
The uniform-gap pattern is inside, not outside.

options.text: the field of a bar magnet
options.explanation: The external pattern runs pole to pole like a magnet's.
That is the single-wire pattern, not a solenoid's.

questions.stem: The field lines INSIDE a solenoid are drawn:

options.explanation: The turns' circles add into the axial field inside.
Field lines never cross.
Radiation is not the solenoid's interior pattern.

options.text: straight, parallel and crowded along the axis
options.explanation: The interior field is strong and uniform.

questions.stem: Which rule names the poles of a solenoid?

options.text: the right-hand grip rule applied to the coil
options.explanation: Curl with the current; the thumb gives the north end.
That rule predicts forces, not solenoid polarity.
A gas law has no role here.

options.text: trial and error with iron filings only
options.explanation: Filings show the pattern; the grip rule names the poles.

questions.stem: A soft iron core is slid inside a current-carrying solenoid. What happens?

options.explanation: The axial pattern is preserved and strengthened.

options.text: the interior field becomes much stronger
options.explanation: The induced core multiplies the field.
Induction strengthens, never weakens, the applied field.
Core insertion changes strength, not polarity.

questions.stem: Which THREE changes all strengthen a solenoid's field?

options.text: more turns, smaller current, steel core left permanent
options.explanation: Smaller current weakens; permanent steel defeats the switch-off.

options.text: longer wire everywhere but same turns and current
options.explanation: Extra length alone adds nothing to the field.

options.text: more turns, larger current, soft iron core
options.explanation: These are the three strength levers.

options.text: fewer turns, larger current, plastic core
options.explanation: Fewer turns weakens; plastic is non-magnetic.

questions.stem: State what a solenoid is.
questions.modelAnswer: A solenoid is a long coil of wire that carries a current and acts like a bar magnet.

questions.stem: State how the right-hand grip rule names the poles of a solenoid.
questions.modelAnswer: Curl the fingers of the right hand with the current around the coil; the thumb points to the north end.

questions.stem: Explain why the interior field of a solenoid is strong and uniform.
questions.modelAnswer: Every turn adds a field contribution in the same axial direction inside the coil, so the contributions stack into a large total. Because the turns are evenly wound, the sum is the same at every interior point along the middle, giving a straight, parallel, equally spaced pattern — a uniform field.

questions.stem: An electromagnet crane uses a solenoid with 200 turns at 4 A on a soft iron core. State two independent upgrades for a stronger lift and one reason a permanent steel core would be a mistake.
questions.modelAnswer: Upgrade the current above 4 A, or add turns above 200 — either lever strengthens the field for a stronger lift. A permanent steel core is a mistake because it would keep holding the scrap after switch-off: the crane could lift but never release.
